Chagee Singapore

Forecast the peak, share the counter

Predictive and physical AI: where to open next, and what the GM decides for the busiest hour
OPIM639  ·  Group 3  ·  Keziah, Jin, Ayumi, Revan  ·  October 2026

Good morning. We are Group 3. Our company is Chagee, and we look at one place in its business: the counter of a Singapore outlet in its busiest hour.

Two kinds of technology meet there. Predictive AI forecasts demand: where to open, and how busy the hour will be. Physical AI, automation and machines, does the fixed steps. Around them, people share the hand steps like a bucket brigade.

Our decision-maker throughout is the GM, Chagee Singapore's general manager. Timing: title and agenda together, about twenty seconds.

Step through four points. One: at group level most revenue comes from franchising, about 88% in FY 2025; company-owned is about 12% and growing fastest. That split is from a secondary source.

Two: Singapore outlets run under one company and one data system. We have this from a Chagee source who asked not to be named; please do not identify them. They told us the ownership form does not matter here because the data sits in one system. That a counter design or roster rule could be rolled out across outlets is our reading, not something we were told.

On the app card: Chagee has an order-ahead, self-pickup app, per its App Store listing, and Vulcan Post reports that Chagee Singapore rolled out in-app ordering and delivery after the long reopening queues. Its Form 20-F for FY 2025 says the business generates and processes personal and transactional data. What we cannot back publicly: the app's share of Singapore orders, and whether searches or location are logged; the App Store privacy label lists precise location as not linked to the user. Those are to confirm with Chagee.

Three: 44 outlets, by the store directory in October (press reports vary: 44–46). Chagee prefers ground-floor mall units.

Four: walk-in, app orders for collection, and third-party delivery orders all end at the same counter. Ordering is app-first: walk-ins order in the app, and the source mentioned counter ordering only as an exception for tourists, which we will confirm. The Chagee app is for ordering ahead and collecting; all delivery goes through third-party apps such as Grab, by the same Chagee source, and there is no Chagee-run delivery. That is why we look at the counter. About fifty seconds.

Our ideation produced three areas. Online retailing is not covered yet and will be added; for now we take two: new stores, for expansion, and the in-store peak.

AI comes in two kinds here. Predictive AI forecasts demand: where a new outlet adds cups, and how busy each hour will be. Physical AI is automation and machines at the counter, from dispensers up to machines that make the drink; that is a type of machine, not a claim about Chagee's plans. Bucket brigade and cross-training are operations tools from Topic 5, order fulfilment, but they decide whether a lean roster actually works.

Every part of the deck is a simulation with a trade-off the GM has to weigh: cups added against cups moved, brigade against fixed posts, a shorter wait against a higher cost, and orders kept against extra labour. The decision-maker is the GM. Today the GM and outlet teams deploy people on local expertise, according to an anonymous Chagee source; the forecast is meant to support those calls, not replace them. About fifty seconds.

04b · Network effectsCourse link · cross-side vs same-side network effects (eBay)

Chagee is not a two-sided platform; its network effects sit on one side, and our AI works on three of them

Our reading: Chagee sells its own tea, so there is no seller side to match. One data loop to grow, two crowding effects to cap.

Where Chagee sits on the diagram · click a loop
  1. 1Customers buy from Chagee's outlets through every channel: a pipeline sale, not a match between two sides.
  2. 2The one network effect we grow, and why we chose Chagee: its sales run through the app, so more app use gives more search and order data, and the forecast and site pick get sharper.
  3. 3Buzz is the same-side plus: a visible queue and posts draw more drinkers. We do not model it.
  4. 4Congestion is the same-side minus: at the peak, each extra customer adds to everyone's wait. Pick a day type on the right.
  5. 5Cannibalisation is the outlets' same-side minus: a new outlet takes cups from its neighbours. Switch the site on the right.
  6. 6Cross-side effects live on others' platforms: delivery apps and malls. Not our lever.
① Grow · predictive AI

Feed the data loop

Why Chagee: app-first and member-led. Group-wide, 257 million registered members (end of June 2026), and members with two or more purchases place more than 78% of orders (earnings call, Aug 2026; SG share to confirm).

Site pick: +731 vs +216 cups a day (synthetic).

② Cap · forecast + counter

Absorb the peak crowd

Forecast crew plus a bucket brigade: event-day walk-aways 54% → 1.2%.

③ Cap · site scoring

Count cups added, not sold

Of 837 cups at the new site, 106 move from nearby outlets. The score subtracts them.

Not our lever

Delivery apps and malls own the cross-side effects; their riders still count in our peak.

Step through
TakeawayMore customers help Chagee only if the map and the counter can absorb them: predictive AI grows the data loop; the forecast, counter design and site score cap congestion and cannibalisation.
OPIM639 · Group 3 · explainer figures are illustrative assumptions · synthetic data

These two areas are connected: more customers generate more data, but they also create queues, while new outlets can take sales from existing ones. Our models examine those trade-offs. A lens from the course: on eBay, buyers and sellers attract each other: a cross-side network effect. Chagee is not that, in our reading: it sells its own tea, so there is no seller side to match. Customers to outlets is a pipeline sale.

What it does have sits on one side. One effect to grow: the data loop, like Netflix. More app users give more searches and orders, so the forecast and the site pick get sharper. This is why we chose Chagee: its business model is app-first and member-led. On its second-quarter 2026 earnings call, Chagee said it had 257 million registered members at the end of June, and that members who made two or more purchases accounted for more than 78% of total orders. Those members sit on Chagee's mobile mini program, its ordering app, according to its first-quarter 2025 results. So nearly every cup leaves a data trail that can feed the loop. These are group-wide figures, not Singapore; Singapore's app share of orders is still to confirm. A same-side plus, buzz: queues and posts draw more drinkers; we do not model it.

And two crowding effects to cap. Congestion: at the peak, every extra customer lengthens everyone's wait; with a normal-day roster on an event day, about 54% of peak-hour orders walk away, and the forecast crew with a bucket brigade brings it to about 1.2%. Cannibalisation: a new outlet takes cups from its neighbours; of 837 cups at the app-search site, 106 move from nearby outlets, against far more beside an existing outlet.

Cross-side effects exist, but on others' platforms: delivery apps and malls. Not our lever. About forty-five seconds.

Where would Outlet #45 add the most cups for Chagee?

Not what a new store sells, but what it adds once you subtract the cups it takes from nearby outlets.

New-store forecast

How it works · DBSCAN on a toy set of searches

OPIM639 · Group 3 · explainer figures are illustrative assumptions · synthetic app data

Chagee Singapore runs on its app, with few kiosks. If Chagee logs searches and their location, which we have to confirm, every search is a demand signal, including searches where no store is close. Here the searches are synthetic. That makes the app the forecasting input for a new store, before it has any sales.

Step one: synthetic app sessions on our map. Gold are within walking distance of an outlet; red found no store nearby. Step two: DBSCAN, unsupervised machine learning, groups red searches that are dense; scattered ones are noise. Step three: cluster centres are candidate sites.

Step four: click the map to test a site. The card leads with the gain for Chagee, which is the store's sales minus the cups it takes from nearby outlets, and gives a verdict: strong, mixed, or mostly moving cups. Try a pin next to Tampines West CC: it sells, but most of it moves from the two Tampines outlets nearby. Step five: the forecast's peak hour gives the opening roster for the counter on the next slides.

If asked how DBSCAN works, press How it works: it replays the algorithm one search at a time on a toy set. The appendix lists every simulated number.

The three sliders are the only inputs: cluster radius, minimum searches per cluster, and how far people will walk. The data is synthetic; with Chagee's real app logs, the same steps would run unchanged. About one and a half minutes.

Course link, Week 3, Analytics and AI: in the Flashion example, demand for a new store was forecast from similar stores. We ask the same question with a different input: app searches around the site.

Context for the GM: Chagee is looking to expand rapidly in Singapore, and how many stores it is going for is confidential. So the forecast ranks sites; it does not assume a number of openings.

Takeaway: Judge a site by what it adds to Chagee, not what it sells. The top cluster, near Choa Chu Kang, adds about 731 cups a day; a store beside an existing outlet would sell plenty, but about 80% of it is moved from that outlet.

OPIM639 · Group 3 · explainer figures are illustrative assumptions · mechanism in seconds, Week 5 bucket-brigade rules

Same counter, same customers, two sharing rules side by side. The counter is today's split, our scenario, not Chagee's disclosed setup. Robots, the navy boxes, take the order, brew tea and milk, and shake and seal. People do cup and ice, toppings and hand-over.

Left, a bucket brigade: each person carries a cup forward; the last hands it over, walks back and takes over a colleague's cup. Right, fixed stations: each person owns a station.

Press play on an event day. Then set the right side to "slowest on toppings": the queue builds at toppings and customers walk away. The brigade never needed to know who was fast.

Be honest about the other case: add people and fixed stations catch up, or are a little faster. About one minute.

Then click the band to reveal the AI layer on its own. Machines are automation, and here they stay exactly as they are: today's split on both sides. AI means AI-assisted staffing: the demand forecast sets the crew. Equipment, customers and each side's sharing rule are held fixed; only the crew changes. Without AI, the normal-day roster of 1 faces an event day: about 54% of peak-hour orders walk away with a brigade, 54% with fixed posts. With AI, the forecast crew of 2 brings that to 1.2% and 4.1%, for S$402 a day against S$372. The band follows the day you pick. Walk-aways and wait are the peak hour, mean of 20 runs; cost is the day's roster plus machines and leaves out lost sales. All illustrative assumptions.

Course link: the bucket-brigade simulation from Week 5 and Week 6, equipment and technology, inspired this counter replica. Same idea, a different use case.

Takeaway: At the forecast's roster on an event day, the brigade loses about 1.2% of orders; fixed stations lose 4.1% to 35%, depending on who is on toppings.

OPIM639 · Group 3 · explainer figures are illustrative assumptions · robot speeds and costs are assumptions, not Chagee data

This is the GM's decision: which counter steps go to machines. Side A opens on human-only: people do every step. Side B opens on machine-made drink: machines make the drink, people tag the order and hand it over. Both are our illustrative scenarios, not Chagee's disclosed setup. Chagee's own equipment cost is not public; its Singapore relaunch used semi-automated equipment, according to Vulcan Post.

Keep two things apart. Machine automation is the split, the equipment on each side. AI here is AI-assisted staffing: the demand forecast sets the crew. Step four reveals the AI layer on its own. Each side keeps its equipment, customers and sharing rule; only the crew moves from the normal-day roster to the forecast roster. On an event day, all by hand without AI has 2 people, and about 40% of peak-hour orders walk away; with AI the forecast puts on 4, walk-aways fall to 0.0%, median wait 5:32 to 1:24, for S$422 a day against S$361. On the machine-made drink the forecast keeps 1 person, so AI changes nothing there: 7.2% still walk away, and the split table adds a person to meet the limit. In our model, forecasting matters most where people do the work. The band follows the day and the equipment you pick; walk-aways and wait are the peak hour, mean of 20 runs; cost is the day's roster plus machines, without lost sales. Illustrative assumptions throughout.

How to use it: choose a split for each side, or click any station to hand it to a robot or a person, then run the peak hour or press End to compare. Each side starts with the fewest people, from the forecast roster up, that keep walk-aways within 2%.

The table compares five options on the chosen day, mean of 20 runs: today's split, the machine-made drink, all by hand, all robots, and one tea-and-milk machine from the machine ladder in the appendix. In our model, one tea-and-milk machine is the cheapest of the five on every day type, because it lets the roster drop a person off-peak at the cost of one machine unit. All robots is the fastest and the dearest: among these options robots buy a shorter wait, not a lower cost.

Qualify it out loud: these results rest on our assumptions, the machine cost of S$1,909 a month per unit, the wage, the station speeds, the demand curve and a minimum crew of 2 by hand and 1 with machines. One machine beats today's split only while a machine unit costs more than about S$905 a month, with the wage, volume and crews held fixed. Chagee's real machine cost is unknown, so the decision is to pilot one machine against today's split, not to switch. About one and a half minutes.

What is AI hereSupervised learning (ridge regression) from site attributes to cups a day. The labels are the slide 05 engine's synthetic outlets, so the fit flatters; Chagee's real opening history would fit worse. Using Singapore to score another market assumes its customers behave alike: check against the first outlets' actuals.

This is the model behind step three of the framework, actually running. It learns cups a day from a site's attributes, trained on Singapore's 44 outlets. The labels are synthetic, from the slide 05 engine, so read it as the method, not a forecast.

We test it fairly: each outlet is predicted by a model that never saw it. With every input, it misses by about 41 cups a day on average. Now the proxy for a new market: there is no Chagee app history and no outlet network yet, so switch those inputs off. With only population and distance to a town centre, the error grows to about 83 cups a day, still better than guessing the average outlet, about 197.

Then the point of it: where to open in a place with no local data. The right-hand map is a hypothetical city, generated at the same density as our Singapore data. With only the inputs that city has, the model scores every spot and picks the best sites at least 2 km apart, so they do not take sales from each other. Each pick shows its forecast with the error band, and whether it clears break-even at Singapore costs, which stand in until local costs are known. Picks beyond what the model saw in Singapore are flagged. So the model can travel, but only on inputs the new market has, with wide ranges: pilot the top site first and recheck the model against its actuals. That is the continual-learning step on the next slide. About fifty seconds.

A strong-demand site can still fail if rent or staffing is too high, or if it mostly takes sales from our own neighbours.

In practice this needs Chagee's opening history. With about 44 outlets in Singapore the model must stay simple (few attributes, ranges not point values).

Illustrative. Synthetic data, not Chagee data. Chagee's opening history is internal and we do not have it. Cups a day, price and margin are the benefit slide's (slide 11); rent, delivery, utilities and set-up cost are assumptions, not Chagee data.

Six steps from a pin to a go or no-go. Steps three, four and six are where the AI would sit in production: a supervised model for the scores, a similarity search for look-alike outlets, and continual learning as each new outlet reports actuals. On this slide only step five is computed.

The waterfall starts from cups a day times price times margin, the same inputs as the benefit slide: 556 cups a day. Take off the profit neighbours lose, delivery fees, the counter, rent and utilities: about S$16,011 a month net to Chagee, a payback of about 25 months. At the low end of the cups range it loses money, so the call is: Pilot. Move rent, delivery or set-up cost and watch the call change; these are our assumptions, not Chagee data.

The honest point: switch to the pin with an outlet 1.7 km away. It takes 44% of its cups from our own outlets and comes out at −S$2,697 a month, a skip. About forty-five seconds.

Later: reuse in new markets via transfer learning, out of scope.

Backup for slide 11. This answers part c of the brief: how big is the benefit, for Singapore only. Against what: a flat normal-day roster and an all-by-hand counter. Chagee deploys people on local expertise, the GM and outlet teams making the calls, so this baseline is ours, not Chagee's practice.

Lead with orders. On an event day the model keeps about 61 orders per outlet in the peak hour that would otherwise walk away, about S$358 of revenue; on a busy day about 5. Over a year it depends on how many such days there are: our illustrative calendar is 104 busy days, the weekends, and 11 event days, the public holidays. That is an input, not a measurement.

Profit is the second line, using a margin we assume because Chagee does not disclose one. The labour saving is shown separately and never added to revenue. The two levers are run together, not added, because they share the same labour hours. The strip at the top splits the profit: most is counter automation, physical AI, the machine on its own; the forecast, predictive AI, adds a small share on top.

Two crew rules for rostering to the forecast. The walk-away rule adds people until peak-hour walk-aways are within 2%; at our default volume that is exactly the forecast crew. The economic rule adds a person only when the orders kept are worth more than the extra hours. They differ on busy days by hand, where the economic rule adds no one.

Be honest about fragility: most of the profit is the counter's labour saving, and it comes from the model's minimum crew, 2 by hand and 1 with machines. Drop that rule and the profit falls to about S$8,395 a year per outlet. And rostering to the forecast pays on event days, not on busy days, where the extra hours cost more than the orders won back. These are modelled avoided costs on stated assumptions, not demonstrated savings. About one minute.

Takeaway: Most modelled profit is counter labour, and it rests on the minimum-crew rule (S$24,660 falls to S$8,395 a year per outlet without it). The forecast pays on event days; on busy days only the economic rule avoids a loss.

Appendix · How the site forecast works (slide 05)

DBSCAN finds where searches bunch up; a proximity model turns a pin into cups

DBSCAN in four moves · toy example
  1. 1Radius ε. Two searches are neighbours if they are within ε of each other (the cluster-radius slider).
  2. 2Core. A search with at least the minimum number of searches within ε (counting itself) is a core point.
  3. 3Grow. A cluster spreads from core to core. Searches it reaches that are not core join as border points.
  4. 4Noise. Searches no cluster reaches. Unlike k-means, nobody picks the number of clusters, and odd shapes are fine.

Unsupervised: no labels or past openings are needed. Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu (1996). On slide 05 it runs only on searches with no outlet within walking distance; each cluster's centre is a candidate site.

The simulated numbers, in order · at the slider defaults
1App searchesSynthetic dots on land: 15% spread evenly, 35% around the outlets' malls, the rest around 20 towns3,000 dots
2No store nearbyThe nearest outlet is further than the walking distance1 km · 46% of dots
3DBSCANClusters the no-store-nearby dotsε 0.6 km · min 15 · 11 clusters
4Pull of a storeFades with distance d: exp(−½ (d/L)²), with the length L set by the walking distanceL = 1 km
5Who buys whereA dot buys at a store in proportion to its pull, against the pull of not buying (a store next door = one)not buying 0.3
6CalibrationEach dot's weight is set so the average outlet sells the deck's cups a day (cups a year ÷ open days)556 cups a day
7Score a pinCups for Chagee = what the new store sells − what it moves from nearby outletstop: 837 − 106 = +731
8VerdictShare of the new store's cups that are new to Chageestrong ≥ 60% · weak < 40%
9Opening rosterPeak-hour cups ÷ cups one person handles, with the safety marginone per 83 cups

All synthetic: the dots, towns and weights are assumptions on the team's map (not to scale), not Chagee app logs or population data. With real app logs, steps one and two change; the rest runs unchanged.

OPIM639 · Group 3 · explainer figures are illustrative assumptions · synthetic app data

Backup for questions on slide 05. Left: DBSCAN in four moves on a toy set. A search is a core point if enough searches sit within the radius; clusters grow from core to core; border points join; the rest is noise. We do not choose the number of clusters.

Right: every simulated number, in the order the model uses it. The forecast is only as good as these assumptions; with Chagee's real app logs, the first two rows would be replaced by data and the rest would run as is.

Assumptions (assumptions.json, illustrative)

Cups per outlet per year: 200000 cups/store/year

Share of the day's cups in each open hour: 0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.11, 0.08, 0.08, 0.09, 0.1, 0.1, 0.09, 0.08, 0.07 share of daily cups per open hour (10:00 to 22:00), sums to 1

Busy and event day multipliers: none 1, moderate 1.5, large 2.5 x forecast arrival rate

Busiest hours the multiplier lands on: 2 busiest forecast hours that get the surge

Seconds per cup by hand, per station: ticket 5, cup ice 10, tea milk 15, topping finish 12, shake seal 10, handover 8 seconds of one average worker per cup

Seconds per cup by robot, per station: ticket 2, cup ice 8, tea milk 10, topping finish 15, shake seal 8, handover 6 seconds per cup per machine unit

Stations the robots do today: ticket, tea milk, shake seal

Spread of worker speeds: 0.2 +/- share around average speed

Minute-to-minute variation in pace: 0.25 coefficient of variation, minute to minute

Share of new staff: 0.25 share of roster in first months

New staff speed: 0.7 x average speed

Coordination loss, people around robots: 0.9 multiplier on human-pool throughput in the mixed setup

Minimum people on the counter: all human 2, mixed 1, all machine 0 workers per open hour

Roster safety margin over the forecast: 1.2 x forecast peak rate

Labour cost per hour worked (SGD): 15.06 SGD per hour worked, fully loaded (statutory costs)

Robot cost per station unit per month (SGD): 1908.75 SGD per station machine unit per month

Attendant hours, all-robot counter: 1 workers per open hour

Walk-away limit for the GM's split table: 0.02 share of peak-hour orders that walk away

Synthetic app-intent dots (slide 05): 3000 synthetic app-intent dots on the map

Walking distance to collect: 1 km a customer will walk to collect

Distance decay, share of the walking distance: 1 distance decay length as a share of walk_km

Pull of not buying: 0.3 pull of not buying, against a store next door (= 1)

DBSCAN cluster radius: 0.6 km

DBSCAN minimum searches: 15 dots within eps to form a cluster core

Map scale: 0.033 km per map pixel

Wait at which a customer walks away: 5 minutes

Price per cup, in store (slides 09, 11): 5.9 SGD per cup, in store

Margin per cup, share of price (slides 09, 11): 0.6 share of price (contribution per avoided order: price minus ingredients and packaging)

Busy days a year (slide 11, illustrative): 104 busy days a year (day type 'moderate')

Event days a year (slide 11, illustrative): 11 event days a year (day type 'large')

Walking-back speed (Week 5 units): 6 lines per hour

Site scores, hand-set (slides 08, 09, illustrative): demand 84, delivery 78, competition 61 score out of 100

Site score weights (slide 09, illustrative): demand 0.5, delivery 0.2, competition 0.3 weight in the site score, sums to 1

Rent per outlet per month (slide 09, assumption, not Chagee data): 15000 SGD per outlet per month

Utilities per outlet per month (slide 09, assumption): 2500 SGD per outlet per month

Share of cups via delivery apps (slide 09, assumption): 0.3 share of the outlet's cups sold through third-party delivery apps

Delivery platform commission (slide 09, assumption): 0.3 share of a delivery order's price paid to the platform

Set-up cost per new outlet (slide 09, assumption, not Chagee data): 400000 SGD per new outlet, one-off (fit-out, equipment, deposits, opening)

Claims we did not make

No Chagee sales, staffing or wait-time data is used; the forecast is not a trained model. We do not claim the bucket brigade always beats fixed stations: with spare staff, a well-assigned fixed line is as good or slightly faster. Machine breakdowns, breaks and order mix are not modelled.

We make no claim about: Singapore ownership structure (an anonymous Chagee source says outlets run under one company and one data system, and that the ownership form does not matter here; I-chagee-contact); delivery profit by channel; Chagee's own equipment cost (not public); gross margin per cup (our assumption); Chagee's current rostering beyond what an anonymous Chagee source told us (people are deployed on local expertise by the GM and outlet teams; slide 11's baseline is ours).
